These are the 3 reasons why your content is not driving leads.

I’ve built three 7-figure businesses from just my organic content.

If you’re struggling to turn those views into dollars, these are your 3 problems.

Number 1…your content is attracting a non-buyer.

If you go too broad, or talk about too many diverse topics, the algorithm will bring you the wrong viewer.

This is a very common mistake.

In this case your biggest issue is topic selection.

Reason Number 2 you can’t drive leads…the viewer doesn’t trust you.

Trust is the new currency of the internet.

If you don’t elicit trust in your content, you’re cooked.

Now trust comes from two things… 

Proof of results or live demonstration of ability.

If you have results, mention them more often in your content.

The best place to put them is in the lock-in zone, the 2-3 sentences after the hook.

If you don’t have results, you need to demonstrate your skills in the content itself.

To do this, your information needs to be nonobvious and tactically implementable.

It has to be new and easy for them to apply on their own.

Reason number 3 why you can’t drive leads…viewers don’t think you’re different enough from the field.

People buy when they think your method will get them a return on their money.

Typically, they have tried other methods in the past that haven’t worked.

If you are just a derivative of everyone else, they will not buy because it’s more of the same.

This means you need to have ideas, methods, and frameworks that are different than everyone else.

I’ve worked 1 on 1 with hundreds of businesses, these are the 3 reasons why their content doesn’t drive leads.

This guy Nate, went from 10K to 500,000 followers in literally 1 month.

These are the 3 most nonobvious hacks he used to speedrun his growth.

Number 1 is using Identity Labels.

In all of his biggest videos, he uses terms like Intellectual Omnivore, Analytical Empath, or Dialectical Thinkers, to describe certain types of people.

Now these labels hit the brain similar to a horoscope.

When you hear them, if they match how you see yourself, you get really excited and engage aggressively.

This is a super powerful psychology concept to build common ground at scale.

Btw, this same principle can be applied in literally every niche and will crush the same.

The second reason why he grew so fast is Series Familiarity.

Most of his top videos are all shot with the exact same visual approach.

It’s him, good lighting, outside, leaning up against a wall.

Most people are afraid to use the same visual setup in every video because they think it will be repetitive.

But you have to remember, viewers are seeing hundreds or thousands of videos between each of yours.

The redundancy in visual format is actually a feature, not a bug.

The third reason why he grew is called Demeanor Matching.

Nate’s audience are people that are super smart gifted thinkers.

And his delivery comes off like a vulnerable smart nerd.

That is a perfect match with the type of people he’s attracting.

And this is key…

It’s not that you have to deliver like he does…

It’s that your delivery has to match closely to the target audience you’re trying to attract.

These are the 6 best content formats for boring businesses.

And if you execute these well, they drive a ton of leads.

Number 1 is “Case Study Projects”

In these videos, you retroactively analyze a project you just did.

Backyard pool build, landscaping, home design, website design…anything you can show visually and walkthrough the process will work.

Number 2 is “Live Work Execution”

In these videos, you voice over footage of you in the trenches doing the work.

As you complete the work, people will realize they want something similar and look to reach out.

Number 3 is “Scenario Build”

In these videos, you walkthrough a hypothetical project.

Things like architectural drawings, renders, schematics, blueprints…

Anything that you’re already doing for prospective clients that fell through could work well here

Number 4 is “Show The Factory/Manufacturing”

In these videos, you take viewers behind the scenes into the factory or manufacturing plant.

The visuals will feel super unique and give a BTS perspective.

Number 5 is Extremes.

Take an example project, but make it the most extreme one you could possibly find.

Powerwashing the dirtiest deck, building the biggest possible door.

Extremes tend to go more viral.

Number 6 is S-Tier Ranking, but specifically for the details, methods, or other brands in your space.

Actually rank a nuanced list where a potential buyer can clearly see you know what you’re talking about.

This is one of the easiest techniques for becoming a better storyteller.

It’s called using Anchor Terms.

I’ve gotten billions of views on my content, and this is one of the core principles I always use.

When you introduce a new concept, the easiest way to build understanding is by relating it to an existing thing the viewer already knows.

You’re anchoring something new, to something known.

For example…

If I were teaching you about how social media algorithms work, I might relate it to a casino and how they use different psychology tricks to hook gamblers.

A casino and gambling is something you already know…so that becomes a helpful frame for this new thing…algorithms.

Building this comparative relationship between terms is a cheat code in increasing comprehension in stories.

And when comprehension goes up, so do the views.

So here’s what you do…

Whenever you’re introducing something new, ask yourself…what is something else that works in a similar way that a lot more of my audience already understands.

Then, frame that comparison as early as possible in the story.

It sounds basic, but I’m telling you, this one little change will dramatically increase your content performance and conversion.

The reason your videos are flopping is because you’re using way too much borrowed authority.

I’ve worked on dozens of high-profile personal brands and this is a huge problem I see.

There are 3 types of authority you can build in your videos:

1. Demonstrated Authority
2. Owned Authority
3. Borrowed Authority

These signal trust in this order…demonstrated is the best and borrowed is the worst.

Demonstrated Authority is when you share proof of results you’ve gotten for others.

Owned Authority is when you share proof you’ve gotten for yourself.

And Borrowed Authority is when you justify something that someone else proved was good.
For example, imagine my hook was something like…

“This is the only storytelling framework you need to get 1M view videos”

In my next line, I want to add proof that validates what I’m about to say.

Demonstrated Authority would be saying…I taught 5 people this and they all got million view videos in their first 2 weeks.

Owned Authority would be saying…I personally used this and got millions of views in my first 2 weeks.

But Borrowed Authority would be something like…Hormozi talks about this and he used it to get a 1M views

In this era, borrowed authority is no longer enough to build trust because everyone can use the same examples.

And rather than trust a derivative curator, I’d rather just go directly to the original source.

Now as a beginner when you don’t have results, it’s okay to start with borrowed authority, but you need to sprint to using your own results if you want to separate from the crowd.

It’s very tough to win if your authority is being built off the back of someone else’s proof.

The true secret to great storytelling is using one of these 5 tricks.

They’re called Psychology Attention Triggers.

And each one is specifically designed to hijack the viewer’s attention.

Number 1 is Extreme Size and Speed.

You want to frame an extremely large result that took a shockingly small amount of time to achieve.

For example, “I planned 60 days of content in just 30 minutes.”

The more extreme on both sides, the better.

Number 2 is specific numbers or dollars.

The more specific and larger the amount, the better.

For example, “I spent $342,000 last year on private jets. Here’s how many rides I took and exactly where I went”

People’s brains can contextualize numbers and dollars much faster than words, which is why this works so well.

Number 3 is specific names of people the viewer wants to be like.

The more closely connected to their ideal future state, the better.

For example, “Shelby Sapp went from $0 to $10M/year in just 3 years. Here’s how she did it…

And if Shelby Sapp is a good representation of who you want to be like, your brain will pay attention much more deeply.

Number 4 is limited experience to drive large results.

And this is similar to number 2.

People want to go from no skills and no money to rich and happy in as short of a time as possible.

If you frame your content as the vehicle to make this happen, it’ll hijack attention.

For example, “here’s how to get your first 1M view video in your first 30 days of posting”

And number 5 is graphics and charts going up and to the right.

Again, people contextualize graphs faster than words, so this makes them opt in quicker.

Use these in either the hook or the lock-in zone right after the hook, and your videos will do much better.

This is the value of every type of follower in 2026.

I call this Audience Math.

10,000 YouTube subscribers is roughly equal to…

* 25,000 email or Substack subscribers
* 50,000 X followers
* 100,000 Instagram followers
* 1M Tiktok followers

Now the truth is, you can make $100K/month with any single one of these…

But here’s how to decide which is best for you to go for.

The first filter is “what type of content naturally suits your personality and skills better?”

If you like writing and prefer to be faceless, go for X first and then parlay that into email.

If you don’t mind being on camera and want to build a personal brand fast, go for short-form video on IG, then parlay that into email.

If you like explaining yourself, are down to grind or have a budget for a team, start with YouTube, then parlay that to email.

Each of these X, IG, and YouTube can all be great funnels into an email list.

And that stack, each + email can easily make 7-figures per year.

Now if it were me, and I could only pick one of these audience, I’d pick a super narrow, super aligned audience on either IG or YouTube.

If I was selling something super high ticket that required explaining and demonstrating my methods, I’d start YouTube long-form then go IG

If I was selling something low to mid ticket that required large social credibility, I’d go IG then use the cashflow to fund YouTube.

The reason your videos don’t hold attention is because you’re completely missing the lock-in zone.

Everybody talks about the hook.

But the real secret sauce are these 2-3 sentences right here.

This is where you actually lock-in a viewer’s attention and get them to stay.

Now there are 6 ways to approach the lock-in zone.

Number 1 is teasing proof.

This is where you’d share a stat or result that supports the claim made in the hook.

Number 2 is teasing a favorable transformation or emotional response.

This is where you’d emphasize the exact before and after result or feeling the viewer will have because of the incoming substance.

Number 3 is adding clarifying contrast.

That’s what I did in this video.

This is where you add contrast against the common belief to clarify that you have something different to say.

Number 4 is introducing the magic box.

This is where you introduce the name of some term, method or framework that they don’t know but want to.

Number 5 is objection handling.

This is when you first make a bold contrarian claim in the hook and then immediately address their most common objection head on to get them to lock back in
And Number 6 is the double down.

This is where you double down on whatever claim you made in the hook to intensify the stance and twist the pain even further.

If you’re not currently approaching your content with a plan for the lock-in zone, this is a big reason why your videos aren’t grabbing attention.

This is one of the best formats for driving leads and sales.

It’s called a Whiteboard Explainer.

Here’s everything you need to make one that actually works to drive conversion.

First, pick your whiteboard layout.

There are 3 main types of whiteboard videos.

Teacher mode, like Gannon and Cat.

Handheld mode, like Yasin.

Or split screen mode, like Briar and Victoria.

Now regardless of which style you pick, there’s one common cheat code across all of these examples.

They all start with something on the board that is covered or unclear.

Could be an unexplained shape or a literal blocker over the words.

This acts like a natural curiosity loop.

And makes you freeze to want to know what’s there.

Make sure you replicate this in your own versions…literally start by blocking the thing on screen and progressively revealing it…but have a text hook or title that is visible.

Now once you start explaining, the Whiteboard works extremely well at building trust because of the subconscious teacher <> student relationship.

Most of us grew up with teachers teaching us in this way.

Seeing the whiteboard shifts your subconscious into a default learning state. 

This is what makes it amazing for lead gen.

Now the hardest part about whiteboard formats is the delivery speed. 

It’s fairly difficult to both write and talk quickly at the same time, so ideally the core points you’re making are already written and you can just talk to them.

This will help speed up the words per minute and increase the speed to value.

So it’s pick your style, block the info, progressively reveal, and increase speed to first value as fast as you can.

The fastest way to get a bigger audience isn’t by going viral.

It’s by making content that is saveworthy.

The more people press save, the more press follow.

It’s that simple.

And the reason is because saving something is a proxy behavior for wanting more in the future…just like a follow.

So here are the 5 best ways to make your content instantly more saveworthy.

Number 1 is clear outcome signaling.

If you bluntly state that this video will have info that helps achieve whatever someone wants, they will be eager to save it.

A video that’s interesting isn’t enough to get a save.

It has to be directly tied to an outcome they want.

Number 2 is having lots of tactical info on the screen.

Typically formats like listicles, tutorials, or breakdowns that show the answer visually in large quantities will be saved.

Number 3 is by intentionally delivering too much tactical info than someone can remember in one shot.

Right around now in a video, your brain gets overloaded and you can’t remember everything.

When this happens, people save if the outcome was signaled.

So you’re intentionally overloading so they have to hit save.

Number 4 is showing specific inputs on screen they’d want later.

Things like set up, prompts, phrases, or key images.

If they want to pause the video and look at those in depth, they’ll have to save for later.

And number 5 is outcome reminders.

As you’re going through, continuing reminding them why this info will help them achieve their goals

Like how this video will help you drive more followers if you execute this list.

Videos that get tons of views have 3 common traits.

Large topic TAM.

Broad hook frame.

Hook frame is how general you make the hook.

Now on the other side, videos that get tons of conversion also have 3 common traits.

Outcome driven.

Super aligned CTA.

Early CTA.

Outcome driven means that you tie the video to the outcome someone wants as early as possible.
I’ll only buy an acne product if you remind me this will solve my acne.

Super aligned CTA means the call for conversion goes to a product or offer that matches the outcome claim.

Early CTA means you find a way to work the CTA into the script as early as possible.

The Goldilocks Format has all 6 of these attributes.

You pick a topic that has a big TAM, make the hook frame broad, and be as concise as possible.

But you also signal the desired outcome, build an aligned CTA and mention it as early as possible.

This is how social media algorithms actually work.

And this’ll explain exactly why certain videos rip and others flop.

When you post a video, the algorithm samples it with a small number of viewers.

Let’s call it 200 people.

Some of those viewers will be existing followers, if you have some.

And the others will be non-followers it thinks would like the video.

Now based on how that first sample group reacts, will determine if the video gets out of 200 view jail.

If the data comes back positive, it’ll push it to an order of magnitude more people, call it 2,000.

If the data comes back neutral, it’ll still push it, but maybe only to another 200 as a 2nd test group.

And if the data comes back negative, it’ll quickly nuke the video.

Remember, the algorithm’s only goal is to keep viewers on the platform.

So if the first set of 200 people didn’t like it, you’re not getting more views because it doesn’t want to risk more unhappy viewers.

Now in order to determine if the data is positive, neutral or negative, the algorithm looks at 3 main things.

The first is average watch time…how long on average did viewers watch for?

The second is engagement rate…what percentage of viewers engaged with the video in any way?

And the third is watch time session share…in a given user’s session, how much of their watch time was spent on your videos?

If you can increase those 3 metrics within the sample group, your videos will do much better.

You must avoid The Viral Trap.

If you’re trying to drive leads and sales with your content, this is the worst thing that can happen to you.

The Viral Trap is when you accidentally go too viral, too soon.

And this sounds like a good problem to have, but it’s actually a death sentence for your channel.

Think of your audience targeting like a bullseye.

The center of the bullseye has topics specifically designed for your ideal viewer.

These are narrow, bottom of funnel videos, made specifically for conversion.

The more you go out from the center, the broader the topics get, and the bigger the potential views.

But here’s what people mess up…

When you go too broad chasing views, you bring in tons of people that are completely outside of your target avatar.
